body.text: On October 22, former Japanese Prime Minister Fukuda Yasuo, aged 90, passed away due to heart failure in Tokyo. Fukuda and his father, Fukuda Takeo, became the first father-and-son pair to serve as prime ministers in the history of Japanese politics.

Fukuda became prime minister on September 26, 2007, at 71 after Abe Shinzo suddenly announced his resignation from the leadership position. From the beginning of his premiership, however, Fukuda struggled for control over policymaking. This was the age of the “twisted Diet,” because the Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) lost its majority in the House of Councillors, Japan’s upper house, in the election of July 2007.

The first priority of the Fukuda administration was to extend the Anti-Terrorism Special Measures Legislation, which would allow the Self-Defense Forces to continue maritime oil refueling missions in the Indian Ocean based on a resolution of the United Nations Security Council. Opposition parties, however, were against the extension.

Since the Democratic Party of Japan (DPJ) held control in the upper house, the legislation – known as the Replenishment Support Special Measures Law – was blocked there. The Fukuda government had to pass it through the lower house, which required a two-thirds majority.

Fukuda considered that the extension of the oil refueling mission in the Indian Ocean was important for the Japan-U.S. military alliance. However, his foreign and security policy emphasized not only the significance of the Japan-U.S. relationship, but also the peace and prosperity of the Asia Pacific region, in accordance with his father’s “Fukuda Doctrine” announced in 1977 in Manila.

During the Koizumi Junichiro government, Fukuda – then chief cabinet secretary – cautioned Koizumi about the negative influence of the prime minister’s official visits to Yasukuni Shrine, where Class A war criminals are enshrined. Fukuda repeatedly stated that Koizumi should not visit Yasukuni Shrine during his premiership out of concern for the relationship with neighboring countries, especially China.
Fukuda’s diplomatic philosophy was reflected in his speech delivered at the 14th International Conference on the Future of Asia held in Tokyo on May 22, 2008.

In the speech, Fukuda stressed the significance of his father’s Fukuda Doctrine and announced “five pledges” to a “future Asia that acts together”: (1) to support ASEAN’s efforts to realize a community, (2) to reinforce the Japan-U.S. military alliance as a form of “public good” in the Asia Pacific, (3) to pursue diplomacy for disaster management cooperation, (4) to facilitate youth exchanges in the Asia Pacific, and (5) to tackle climate change by establishing a low-carbon society. It is noteworthy that the five pledges valued a variety of international cooperation efforts for the maintenance of peace and security, including natural disaster response and environmental issues.

On September 1, 2008, Fukuda announced his resignation from the leadership position. Four years later, on September 26, 2012, Fukuda announced that he would not run for the next general election. When the lower house was dissolved by Prime Minister Noda Yoshihiko on November 16, 2012, Fukuda retired as a politician of the House of Representatives. Fukuda’s constituency was succeeded by his son, Fukuda Tatsuo.

After that, Fukuda Yasuo was appointed as a special envoy by Prime Minister Abe. Along with Prince Naruhito, he attended the funeral of former South African President Nelson Mandela on December 9, 2013.

Fukuda’s peace philosophy can be observed in his policy speeches delivered as prime minister at the Diet. In his general policy speech on October 1, 2007, Fukuda referred to the word “peace” four times, and stated that his government would promote diplomacy based on the Japan-U.S. alliance and international cooperation to contribute to world peace. He explained that it was important for the Self-Defense Forces to continue U.N.-authorized anti-terrorism activities in the Indian Ocean. Fukuda also mentioned the importance of peace in Asia and the necessity of denuclearization of the Korean Peninsula, which influenced the peace and defense of Japan.

In his administrative policy speech on January 18, 2008, Fukuda referred to the term “peace” 10 times, and argued that Japan should become a “peace cooperation state” that could contribute to resolving global issues. Specifically, Fukuda stated that it was necessary for Japan to contribute to international peace cooperation in postwar international activities for the Indian Ocean, Afghanistan, and Iraq. Likewise, he mentioned the necessity to reinforce the diplomatic efforts for nonproliferation of weapons of mass destruction as well as anti-terrorism. Furthermore, Fukuda expressed his view on world peace that Japan’s international peace cooperation should not be limited to security areas, but needs to include such fields as global warming, poverty, and global health issues.

Significantly, Fukuda’s peace philosophy can be seen in his speech delivered as prime minister at the Hiroshima Peace Memorial Ceremony on August 6, 2008. In the speech, Fukuda mentioned the term “peace” 11 times, and pledged that Japan as a “peace fostering nation” should “firmly maintain the Three Non-Nuclear Principles and lead the international community toward the total elimination of nuclear weapons and the realization of a permanent peace.” Likewise, Fukuda supported the establishment of the International Commission on Nuclear Nonproliferation and Disarmament (ICNND) proposed by Australian Prime Minister Kevin Rudd that same year. Thus, Fukuda explicitly showed his antiwar and antinuclear pacifism as Japan’s top leader.

At the same time, Fukuda as prime minister did not visit Yasukuni Shrine. Fukuda instead stated that Japan “inflicted significant damage and pain on many countries, especially on people in Asian countries.” Even after retirement, Fukuda publicly argued that Japanese prime ministers should not pay official visits to Yasukuni Shrine. “China adopted the position that the Japanese who were guilty were war criminals and leaders who started the war, and not ordinary soldiers,” he said. “Japanese people must think about the reality of what a place that enshrines Class A war criminals means.”

Fukuda’s view on Japan’s war responsibility in relation to the Yasukuni Shrine issue is consistent with his father’s Fukuda Doctrine. Indeed, like his father, who promoted the peaceful relationship between Japan and Asian countries, Fukuda valued an amicable Sino-Japanese relationship. Notably, in June 2018, Fukuda visited the Memorial Hall for the Nanjing Massacre in China and offered flowers and a prayer for the deceased. Fukuda expressed his view on the importance of the bilateral reconciliation and history recognition, stating, “On behalf of the people of Japan, I hereby express my feelings of profound remorse and sincere mourning for all the victims of the war… Japanese people need to visit the memorial hall [for the Nanjing Massacre] and understand the history.”
Fukuda offered prayers for the deceased in Japan and China, signifying that he had desired the peace and prosperity of Japan, Asia, and the world.

Moreover, Fukuda had been involved in the InterAction Council, established by Fukuda Takeo with other former world leaders in 1983, which aims to foster international cooperation and action in three priority areas: “peace and security, world economic revitalization, and universal ethical standards.” Importantly, the InterAction Council issued the “Hiroshima Declaration: A Plea for Zero Nuclear Weapons” calling for the abolition of nuclear weapons at the 28th annual plenary meeting held in Hiroshima on April 19, 2010.

On March 26-27, 2014, Fukuda and former Australian Prime Minister Malcolm Fraser co-chaired an international conference, “Interfaith Dialogue: Global Ethics in Decision Making” in Vienna. At the conference, Fukuda emphasized the importance of “tolerance and understanding” to promote interfaith and inter-civilizational dialogues.

Notably, Fukuda mentioned the importance of peace philosophy of Immanuel Kant regarding the maintenance of peace, and finalized his statement with a phrase of Buddha regarding love and hatred. Therefore, Fukuda’s diplomatic philosophy was influenced by his father’s Fukuda Doctrine as well as the pacifist philosophers. Fukuda made efforts to make contributions to the maintenance of international peace and security. Fukuda’s peace philosophy became more profound after he resigned from the position of prime minister, and he had continued his political activities toward the world without war and nuclear weapons.
This article is based on a chapter of the author’s book, “Japanese Prime Ministers and Their Peace Philosophy” (Palgrave Macmillan, 2022) and is used with permissions.
